Delboeuf

CirclesGeometryParadoxes
Game: Two coloured circles look different in size, but the drawing gives them exactly the same size.
How to play: Move the five sliders to change the circles and what surrounds them. Drag the probe dot, or focus it and use the arrow keys, to check a ring.

Keyboard: Tab to the probe dot, then use the arrow keys (Shift makes a bigger step). Each slider also has arrow keys.

Look for the math

The cut-the-knot page says: "Two equal circles - one inside a bigger circle, the other containing a smaller circle - seem to have different sizes." The surprise is only in the seeing. The drawing code gives the two coloured circles exactly the same numbers; the logic test checked that over every setting of the three size sliders.

Two circles with the same recipe

The applet first takes a step u = round(width / 5) and then s4 = round(u × MR / 200) and s5 = round(s4 × WR / 100). Both coloured rings are drawn with radius s4 + s5 and edge width s5, and both get the same colour. Moving the circle that surrounds them, or the one inside them, never changes those two numbers. At the opening values on a 500-unit board, u = 100, s4 = 25, s5 = 3, so each coloured ring has radius 28. The test compared all 186,550 MR × DR × WR settings with a second transcription of the bytecode: the two coloured circles matched in every one.

The neighbours are what change

Let s6 = round(s4 × DR / 100). The black ring around the left circle has radius s4 + s5 + s6; the black circle inside the right one has radius s4 - s6 - s5. With the opening settings these are 31 and 19, so the page's description is literally true: bigger outside on the left, smaller inside on the right. Across all 186,550 size settings on this board the smaller-inside relation never failed. The bigger-outside relation failed in 7,831 settings, exactly those where Java's rounding makes s6 = 0 (small MR together with small DR): then the two left rings have the same radius. The page does not mention that edge case, and this port keeps it. At the most extreme MR = 10, DR = WR = 50 the last radius works out to -1; the applet asks Java for a negative-size oval and paints nothing, so the SVG hides that ring instead.

The other two sliders

The guide-shade slider is the applet's CI field. At 255 it draws no lines; at any other value it draws two horizontal lines at mid - s4 - trunc(s5/2) - 1 and mid + s4 + trunc(s5/2), using a shade scaled by CI / 255. The tint slider is Ci: positive mixes the foreground towards red, negative towards blue, in steps of one percent, so Ci = 100 is pure red and Ci = -100 pure blue. The live page passes fcolor=000000 and bcolor=ffffff to the applet, which is why the rings start black and the panel white; this port uses the site's ink and stage colours so both themes stay readable. The test checked every one of the 261 guide shades and all 201 tints against the bytecode, plus 13,251 pairs of them together.

What the eye adds

The page calls this an assimilation illusion: copies of a shape seem to take on properties of their surroundings. It is an optical illusion, not a trick in the numbers. No pixel test can measure how big a circle looks, so the test checks what it can: the two coloured circles are drawn identically, and only their neighbours and colours change. Use the probe dot to put numbers on what your eyes are disagreeing about.

Try setting the outside-size slider to 10 and the inside-size slider to 1: both coloured circles shrink together to radius 8, and the bigger ring around the left one has disappeared.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
